title: Supplied Claim: Manafort Helped Russia Take Crimea
date_status: Supplied date; no source ties this date to a specific Manafort action.
description_short: TrumpFile alleges Manafort helped Russia take Crimea in 2014; the supplied Vox link does not name Manafort or establish that role.
description_medium: TrumpFile's March 16, 2014 entry alleges that Paul Manafort helped Russia take control of Crimea through an illegal vote and cites a Vox explainer. The Vox article describes the referendum under Russian military occupation but does not mention Manafort. No supplied source identifies an action by him or connects him to the takeover; keep the allegation unverified.
description_long:
The supplied TrumpFile page labels the event March 16, 2014 and says Russia took control of Crimea “with help from Paul Manafort” through an “illegal vote.” Its only linked reference in the packet is a Vox explainer about the 2014 Ukraine crisis. That article describes Crimea’s March referendum as taking place without international monitors and under Russian military occupation, but it does not name Manafort or attribute a role in the seizure to him.

The available record documents an allegation made by the TrumpFile page, not independent support for Manafort’s alleged assistance. The packet identifies no action, date, intermediary, or mechanism by which he could have aided Russia’s takeover. Manafort’s political work in Ukraine, even where reported, would not by itself establish involvement in Crimea’s occupation or referendum. This draft keeps the supplied allegation visible for review and makes no finding that it occurred.

The March 16 date remains supplied rather than verified as the date of a specific Manafort action. The link to Donald Trump is also unresolved in this event record. To treat the claim as a historical event, a reliable source must identify a specific Manafort action and connect it to Russia’s control of Crimea; otherwise the entry should be narrowed or excluded.

title: March 24 OMB Funding Freeze Put BIS Emergency Funds at Issue
description_short: OMB's March 24, 2025 action withheld emergency funding that senators said included $20 million for BIS, prompting questions about export-control capacity.
description_medium: On March 24, 2025, OMB recommended that the President withhold designation from 11 emergency appropriations. Senate Banking Democrats said the decision withheld $20 million allocated to the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), about 10.5 percent of its budget, and asked how export-control work would be affected. March conference reporting described an enforcement ramp-up, so the supplied claim that BIS enforcement and prosecutions ended is unsupported.
description_long:
On March 24, 2025, the White House issued a presidential message and OMB memorandum designating 16 emergency appropriations while declining to designate 11 others. A March 27 Senate Banking Committee release said the action withheld $20 million appropriated to the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which the senators described as 10.5 percent of the agency’s budget. Their letter warned that the reduction could affect export-control work and requested information about the legal rationale, operational impact, and any staffing or spending plans. Those warnings are attributed to the senators; the sources do not establish that BIS enforcement had been dismantled or that prosecutions stopped.

A March 2025 account of BIS’s annual export-control conference described officials discussing increased enforcement, technology investigations, and cooperation with the Justice Department to prosecute diversions destined for Iran. Reuters later reported a backlog of export-license applications amid agency turmoil and noted that Commerce defended its reviews as “no longer a rubber stamp.” That later licensing disruption does not show that prosecutions ended in March.

This corrected entry records the funding action and the concerns it prompted. It does not repeat the original assertions that enforcement staff were fired or cases involving China, Russia, and Iran were halted. The sources support a funding dispute and a risk raised by senators, not a measured collapse in BIS enforcement or a finding that the funding decision was unlawful.

title: Trump Demands Sotomayor and Ginsburg Recuse from Trump-Related Cases
description_short: On Feb. 25, 2020, Trump called for Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ruth Bader Ginsburg to recuse from Trump-related matters.
description_medium: On Feb. 25, 2020, Trump demanded that Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ruth Bader Ginsburg recuse from all Trump-related matters. ABC News tied the demand to criticism of Sotomayor's dissent in a case involving an administration policy. The supplied entry misdates the event to 2025, substitutes Ketanji Brown Jackson for Ginsburg, and adds an unsupported racism claim.
description_long:
ABC News reported that on February 25, 2020, President Donald Trump called for two Supreme Court justices to recuse themselves from all Trump-related matters. He named Sonia Sotomayor and Ruth Bader Ginsburg and wrote, “Both should recuse themselves on all Trump, or Trump related, matters!” The article placed the demand after Sotomayor criticized the Court’s handling of a Trump administration policy and reported that Trump said the justices had treated him unfairly.

This is a public demand directed at sitting justices. The source does not establish that either justice recused in response, that the Court changed its procedures, or that a case outcome changed because of the statement. ABC also notes that justices decide for themselves when recusal is appropriate.

The supplied entry’s February 2025 date and reference to Ketanji Brown Jackson do not match the documented event: the source identifies Ruth Bader Ginsburg and dates the demand to February 25, 2020. The source supports a recusal demand and an accusation of unfair treatment; it does not support the separate claim that Trump accused the justices of racism. This repair describes the reported demand without implying that it caused a ruling or actual recusal.
